source.title: Questioning Representational Optimism in Deep Learning: The Fractured Entangled Representation Hypothesis
source.authors: Akarsh Kumar; Jeff Clune; Joel Lehman; Kenneth O. Stanley

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses polysemanticity and superposition, but its own experiments study representation organization in image-generating CPPNs, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether those responses share a feature.
record.gate_note: The paper cites other studies and gives behavioral examples of possible fractured representations in language and image models; those are not its own experimental results and are not rows. Its own CPPN visualizations, weight sweeps, and PCA comparison report on internal representation organization, not the polysemantic-neuron behavior measured by the claim versions; these are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper's own experiments visualize internal activation maps and weight sweeps of image-generating CPPNs (Picbreeder vs SGD). It never measures whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, nor the share of such neurons, their cause, or their measurement dependence. Polysemanticity and superposition are mentioned only in one discussion paragraph, which calls them likely consequences of FER, with no supporting result. So it tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors argue that identical output can hide very different internal representations: SGD-trained CPPNs show fractured entangled representation (FER), while Picbreeder-evolved CPPNs approach unified factored representation. They speculate that FER may exist in large models and degrade generalization, creativity and continual learning, so 'representational optimism' merits scrutiny. In passing, they also say superposition and polysemanticity are likely consequences of FER, but they offer no test of this.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares visualized CPPN neuron activation maps and weight perturbations in a toy image-generation task; it does not apply the original neuron-polysemanticity measurement to unrelated image categories or language-model contexts.
record.method_sensitivity: The PCA basis gives a slightly less fractured-looking representation than the ordinary basis, though the authors say it remains far from the Picbreeder representation. They also report that the qualitative FER finding persists in their ReLU-only CPPNs.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD-trained CPPNs match target images but show disorganized, redundant intermediate activation maps and incoherent weight-sweep effects. Picbreeder-evolved CPPNs with identical output show organized, symmetric maps and semantic sweeps. This holds for skull, butterfly and apple, and for ReLU-only SGD nets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks trained by conventional SGD to a fixed objective develop fractured, entangled representations despite matching output, unlike open-ended evolved networks.

fits_no_version.finding: A PCA rotation of the SGD skull features looks slightly less fractured but remains far from the Picbreeder organization. Random-direction weight-column sweeps still show meaningless distortions for SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The apparent disorganization of SGD CPPN representations is not removed by a change of feature basis.

record.problems: The main experiments use a toy CPPN task with a small set of image targets. The representation and weight-sweep findings are primarily qualitative; selected weight sweeps were chosen to present both methods in their best light, though the paper says they are broadly representative and provides all sweeps at the code link. The paper does not empirically test whether these observations transfer to large models or to polysemantic-neuron measurements.
record.rows_left_out: No own results on the paper's cited language-model examples or cited mechanistic-interpretability studies were entered as rows; they are reports of other work. The CPPN studies of butterfly and apple are omitted because they add further examples of the same adjacent representation-organization finding but do not test a claim version; the paper presents them in Appendix D, Figures 14–20.

untested.parts: No image-classifier neurons; CPPN neurons map coordinates to colors, with no unrelated input categories.
No LM MLP neuron measurements; LM examples are behavioral anecdotes or cited work.
Superposition is asserted to be a consequence of FER in discussion only; not tested.
No test of polysemanticity with sufficient capacity.
The ReLU vs mixed-activation comparison concerns FER, not polysemantic neuron share or its performance cost.
No inspection of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No varying of activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: This is a position paper. Its only contact with the claim is one discussion sentence attributing polysemanticity to FER, with citations to Olah 2020 (an original source) and Elhage 2022. The LLM behavioral examples (GPT-3 counting, GPT-4o word replacement, ape thumb) are anecdotal 3-trial probes of FER, not neuron measurements. The butterfly and apple appendix results extend the same FER finding.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neurons or unrelated image categories such as cat faces and car fronts are tested.
No transformer language-model MLP neurons, token/context responses, or layerwise shares of polysemantic neurons are measured.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure or superposition causes polysemantic neurons.
The study does not test polysemantic neurons arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

Although it compares CPPN representation visualizations across activation/architecture settings, it does not measure polysemantic-neuron shares or test whether they can be reduced without substantial performance loss.
The study does not inspect canonical polysemantic neurons to determine whether their mixed responses detect a shared feature.
The study does not measure how polysemanticity classifications vary with activation range or explanation-scoring method.

rows.subject: Conventional SGD CPPN (skull)
rows.operation_detail: Visualized neuron activations over the input coordinate grid, layer by layer.
rows.measure: Qualitative organization of intermediate neuron activation maps.
rows.baseline: Picbreeder CPPN representation of the same skull
rows.value: Text describes the SGD representation as a disorganized patchwork with many more novel patterns than necessary; it says the two sides are not encoded symmetrically until the output layer.
rows.note: This is evidence about representation organization in a toy image generator, not a measurement of neurons responding to unrelated categories of input.

rows.subject: Picbreeder CPPN (skull)
rows.operation_detail: Visualized neuron activations over the input coordinate grid, layer by layer.
rows.measure: Qualitative organization of intermediate neuron activation maps; count of novel representations stated in the text.
rows.value: The representation is described as organized and symmetric across layers; the layerized CPPN has 24 novel representations.
rows.note: The 24 count refers to novel representations in the layerized Picbreeder CPPN, not to polysemanticity.
rows.check: Comparator description of the Picbreeder CPPN. The '24 novel representations' count describes encoding efficiency, not polysemanticity. State 'observed' has no version to be observed against.

rows.subject: Conventional SGD CPPN (skull)
rows.operation_detail: Swept individual network weights and observed changes to the generated image.

conditions.value: selected single-weight sweeps; authors state selected sweeps were chosen to present both methods in their best light and were broadly representative

rows.measure: Qualitative coherence and semantic interpretability of output changes under weight sweeps.
rows.value: The text says the SGD weight sweeps produce meaningless distortions and almost always break symmetry incoherently; it states all SGD weights lead to similarly meaningless perturbations.
rows.note: Qualitative weight-perturbation evidence about the toy network's representation; not a test of mixed neuron responses to unrelated inputs.

rows.subject: Picbreeder CPPN (skull)
rows.operation_detail: Swept individual network weights and observed changes to the generated image.
rows.measure: Qualitative coherence and semantic interpretability of output changes under weight sweeps.
rows.value: The selected sweeps are described as producing meaningful semantic changes while generally preserving overall symmetry; one shown sweep produces an orderly winking change that disrupts symmetry.
rows.note: Comparator result about weight-space adaptability in a toy network, not neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: Comparator weight-sweep result. Sweeps were hand-selected to show each method in its best light, so this is not a rate measure. It bears on no version.

rows.subject: Conventional SGD CPPN (skull)
rows.operation_detail: Projected each layer's latent data onto principal components and visualized the transformed feature dimensions.

conditions.value: PCA of each layer's latent data

rows.measure: Qualitative organization of the transformed intermediate representations.
rows.value: The PCA view is described as slightly less fractured, but still far from the Picbreeder CPPN's UFR.
rows.note: The study reports a change in representation appearance under a different basis, but does not classify neurons as polysemantic under either view.
rows.check: PCA basis view. A basis-dependence result on representation organization, not on neuron polysemanticity classification (V7). Correctly linked to none. The weight-column sweeps in Fig. 25 are actually on the skull per Appendix F text, though the caption says butterfly; this is not recorded.

rows.subject: Conventional SGD CPPN (skull, ReLU architecture)
rows.stage_stated: trained with SGD; iteration count not stated for this appendix result
rows.operation_detail: Visualized intermediate neuron activation maps in a standard MLP using only ReLU activations.
rows.measure: Qualitative organization of intermediate activation maps.
rows.value: The text says the ReLU network still exhibits FER, with skull-shaped maps containing erratic high-frequency artifacts that cancel at the output.
rows.note: This concerns FER in an image-generating toy network, not polysemantic-neuron frequency.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
